section-77: Smith's wealth definition (1776) treated economics as the study of how nations become rich through production, division of labour and trade. It was criticised as materialistic. Robbins's scarcity definition (1932) made economics a science of choice: because wants are unlimited and resources are scarce with alternative uses, people must choose.
The shift from Smith to Robbins shows how the subject moved from wealth to welfare (Marshall) and then to scarcity and choice, making economics applicable to every society and every individual.
section-78: What to produce means deciding which goods and how much of each to produce with limited resources. How to produce means choosing between labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques. For whom to produce means deciding how output is distributed among households.

These problems are common to all economies. They are illustrated by the production possibility curve, which shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce, and the opportunity cost of producing more of one good.
section-79: The law of demand states an inverse relation between price and quantity demanded, while the law of supply states a direct relation between price and quantity supplied, other things remaining the same.

Equilibrium price is fixed where demand equals supply. If price is above equilibrium there is excess supply and price tends to fall; if price is below equilibrium there is excess demand and price tends to rise. Changes in demand or supply shift the equilibrium.
section-80: Important concepts are Gross Domestic Product (GDP), Gross National Product (GNP = GDP + net factor income from abroad), Net National Product (NNP = GNP - depreciation) and National Income (NNP at factor cost). Per capita income is national income divided by population.

It is measured by three methods: product (value added) method, income method and expenditure method. In India the National Statistical Office (NSO) under MoSPI estimates national income. Difficulties include the non-monetised sector, lack of data, double counting and informal activities.
section-81: A balanced budget has receipts equal to expenditure; a surplus budget has receipts greater than expenditure; a deficit budget has expenditure greater than receipts. Modern governments often use deficit budgets to promote growth and employment.

The budget has two parts: the revenue budget (revenue receipts and revenue expenditure) and the capital budget (capital receipts and capital expenditure). Important deficit measures are revenue deficit, fiscal deficit and primary deficit.
section-82: Under Article 112 of the Constitution, the Union Budget is called the 'Annual Financial Statement'. It is prepared by the Ministry of Finance and presented in Lok Sabha by the Finance Minister, usually on 1 February.

Stages of passing: presentation, general discussion, scrutiny by departmental committees, voting on demands for grants, passing of the Appropriation Bill and passing of the Finance Bill (for tax proposals). No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India without parliamentary approval.
section-83: Tax revenue includes direct taxes such as income tax and corporation tax, and indirect taxes such as GST, customs and excise duties. Non-tax revenue includes interest receipts, dividends and profits of public enterprises, fees, fines, and grants.

Public revenue is needed to finance government functions, reduce inequality through progressive taxation and influence economic activity. A good tax system follows canons such as equity, certainty, convenience and economy.
section-84: Public expenditure can be classified into revenue and capital expenditure, development and non-development expenditure, and plan and non-plan expenditure (older classification). Examples include defence, interest payments, subsidies, education, health and infrastructure.

Wagner's law states that public expenditure tends to increase as an economy develops. Public expenditure promotes growth, provides public goods, redistributes income and stabilises the economy during recessions.
section-85: Main characteristics: (1) mixed economy with both public and private sectors; (2) developing economy with growing per capita income; (3) large population and demographic dividend; (4) the services sector contributes the largest share of GDP while agriculture employs a large share of workers; (5) unemployment and underemployment; (6) inequality of income and regional disparities; (7) a large informal sector.

In recent decades India has become one of the fastest-growing major economies, with progress in information technology, digital payments and infrastructure, but challenges remain in poverty, health, education and job creation.
section-86: India is the most populous country in the world. According to Census 2011, India's population was about 121 crore, the decadal growth rate was 17.7 per cent and the sex ratio was 940 females per 1,000 males. Mizoram had a sex ratio of about 976.

Population growth affects food supply, employment, housing, education and health services. A young population can become a demographic dividend if it is educated, healthy and employed. Population policy aims at stabilising population through health, education and family welfare.
section-87: Growth is quantitative and measured by increase in GDP or per capita income. Development is qualitative and includes improvement in health, education, life expectancy, poverty reduction, equality and freedom. Growth is necessary but not sufficient for development.

Development is measured by indicators such as the Human Development Index (HDI), which combines life expectancy, education and per capita income. Sustainable development means meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
section-88: The 1991 reforms followed a balance of payments crisis. Liberalisation reduced licences and controls; privatisation reduced the role of the public sector through disinvestment; globalisation opened the economy to foreign trade and investment.

Results include faster growth, expansion of services and IT, higher foreign exchange reserves and more competition. Critics point to rising inequality, agrarian distress and jobless growth. Later reforms include GST (2017), the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and digital initiatives.
section-90: Definitions: Smith viewed economics as a science of wealth; Marshall as a study of material welfare; Robbins as a science of choice between unlimited ends and scarce means. Scarcity is the root of all economic problems.

Basic problems: Every economy must decide what goods to produce, which technique of production to use and how output is distributed. These are solved through the price mechanism in market economies and through planning in command economies; India uses a mixed approach.

Demand and supply: Demand depends on price, income, prices of related goods, tastes and expectations; supply depends on price, costs, technology and government policy. A change in own price causes movement along a curve, while other factors shift the curve.

Market equilibrium: The equilibrium price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Excess demand pushes the price up and excess supply pushes it down. These simple tools help explain everyday events such as rising vegetable prices during floods or falling prices after a good harvest.
section-91: National income: Concepts include GDP, GNP, NNP and national income at factor cost. Measurement methods are the product, income and expenditure methods. National income data help to assess economic growth, compare living standards and plan policy.

Budget: The Union Budget (Annual Financial Statement, Article 112) contains estimates of receipts and expenditure for the financial year (1 April to 31 March). It is divided into revenue and capital accounts. Deficits include revenue deficit, fiscal deficit and primary deficit.

Budget procedure: Preparation by the Finance Ministry, presentation in Parliament, general discussion, departmental committee scrutiny, voting on demands for grants, the Appropriation Bill and the Finance Bill. This ensures parliamentary control over public finance.

Public revenue and expenditure: Revenue comes from direct taxes, indirect taxes (especially GST) and non-tax sources. Expenditure covers defence, interest, subsidies, salaries, social services and infrastructure. Well-designed fiscal policy promotes growth, equity and stability.
section-92: Characteristics of the Indian economy: India is a developing, mixed economy with a large population, high dependence on agriculture for employment, a rapidly growing services sector, widespread informal employment, regional imbalance and income inequality, along with rapid progress in technology and digital services.

Population: Census 2011 recorded about 121 crore people, a decadal growth rate of 17.7 per cent and a sex ratio of 940. Rapid population growth puts pressure on resources but a young working-age population offers a demographic dividend.

Growth and development: Growth is an increase in real output; development includes better health, education, equality and quality of life, measured by indicators like HDI. Development should also be sustainable.

Economic reforms: The New Economic Policy of 1991 introduced liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation (LPG). It removed industrial licensing, reduced tariffs, opened sectors to foreign investment and reformed the financial sector. Reforms raised growth and modernised the economy, though concerns remain about inequality and employment.
section-96: Phases: (1) indigenous bankers and moneylenders in ancient and medieval India; (2) agency houses and the first banks such as the Bank of Hindustan (1770); (3) the three Presidency Banks of Bengal, Bombay and Madras, merged in 1921 into the Imperial Bank of India, which became the State Bank of India in 1955; (4) establishment of the RBI in 1935.

After independence came nationalisation of 14 major banks in 1969 and 6 more in 1980, which spread branches to rural areas. The Narasimham Committee reforms of 1991 and 1998 opened the sector to private banks and introduced prudential norms. Recent developments include payments banks, small finance banks, bank mergers and digital banking.
section-97: The central bank does not deal with the general public for profit; it works in the public interest. Examples are the Reserve Bank of India, the Bank of England (the oldest modern central bank, 1694) and the Federal Reserve of the USA.
Its main aims are maintaining price stability, ensuring a sound banking system, managing the exchange rate and supporting economic growth.
section-98: Explanation: As the sole bank of issue, the central bank issues currency notes. As banker to the government it keeps government accounts, manages public debt and gives advice. As bankers' bank it keeps cash reserves of commercial banks and supervises them. As lender of last resort it gives loans to banks in crisis. It also acts as custodian of foreign exchange reserves and clearing house.
Its most important function is credit control, through which it regulates the volume and direction of credit to control inflation and promote growth.
section-99: Main instruments: (1) Bank rate - the rate at which the central bank lends long-term to banks; (2) Repo and reverse repo rates - rates for short-term borrowing and absorbing funds; (3) Open market operations - sale and purchase of government securities; (4) Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) - share of deposits banks must keep with the RBI; (5) Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) - share of deposits banks must hold in liquid assets.
To control inflation, the central bank raises these rates and ratios or sells securities, which reduces credit. To encourage growth, it lowers them or buys securities.
section-100: Qualitative or selective methods include fixing margin requirements on loans against securities, regulation of consumer credit, credit rationing, moral suasion (persuasion and advice to banks), direct action against defaulting banks and publicity.
They are used to discourage speculative or unproductive lending and to direct credit toward priority sectors such as agriculture, small industries and exports.
section-101: The RBI was established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act 1934 on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission, and was nationalised in 1949. Its headquarters is in Mumbai and it is managed by a Central Board headed by the Governor.

Functions include issue of currency (except one-rupee notes and coins issued by the government), banker to the government, bankers' bank, controller of credit, custodian of foreign exchange under FEMA, regulator of payment systems and promoter of rural credit and financial inclusion. Since 2016 a Monetary Policy Committee decides the policy repo rate with an inflation target of 4 per cent (with a band of 2 to 6 per cent).
section-102: Monetary policy may be expansionary (cheap money policy), which lowers interest rates and increases credit to promote growth, or contractionary (dear money policy), which raises rates to control inflation.

In India the RBI follows flexible inflation targeting. Its tools include the repo rate, reverse repo, standing deposit facility, marginal standing facility, CRR, SLR and open market operations. Limitations include a large informal sector, time lags and the influence of fiscal policy and supply shocks.
section-103: Crowther defined money as anything generally acceptable as a means of exchange which at the same time acts as a measure and store of value. Money solved the problems of barter, such as lack of double coincidence of wants, lack of a common measure of value and indivisibility of goods.
Money has evolved from commodity money (cattle, grain) to metallic money, paper money, bank money, plastic money and digital money.
section-104: Primary functions: medium of exchange (it facilitates buying and selling) and measure of value (it acts as a common unit of account). Secondary functions: store of value (wealth can be saved in money), standard of deferred payments (loans and future payments are expressed in money) and transfer of value.

Contingent functions include distribution of national income, equalisation of marginal utilities, basis of credit, and providing liquidity. Because of these functions money is called the lifeblood of a modern economy.
section-105: Metallic money includes standard coins (face value equal to metal value) and token coins (face value higher than metal value). Paper money may be convertible or inconvertible (fiat money). Bank or deposit money consists of demand deposits transferable by cheque.

Other classifications include legal tender (limited and unlimited) and optional money, and near money such as bills and bonds. Modern forms include plastic money (cards), e-money and central bank digital currency such as the RBI's e-rupee.
section-106: Primary functions: accepting deposits (savings, current, fixed, recurring) and advancing loans (overdrafts, cash credit, term loans, discounting of bills). Secondary functions include agency services (collecting cheques, paying bills, buying and selling securities) and utility services (lockers, letters of credit, remittances, foreign exchange).

Commercial banks in India include public sector banks, private sector banks, foreign banks, regional rural banks, small finance banks and payments banks. They mobilise savings and channel them into productive investment.
section-107: Process: When a bank receives a primary deposit it keeps a part as reserve (cash reserve ratio) and lends the rest. The loan is spent and returns to the banking system as a new (derivative) deposit, which is again partly lent. This repeated process multiplies deposits.

Credit multiplier = 1/required reserve ratio. For example, with a 10 per cent reserve ratio, an initial deposit of Rs 1,000 can create total deposits of Rs 10,000. Limits include the reserve ratio, cash leakage, banking habits, demand for loans and availability of securities.
section-108: Savings deposits earn interest and allow limited withdrawals; they suit individuals. Current deposits are used mainly by businesses, allow unlimited transactions and overdrafts, but usually pay no interest. Fixed (term) deposits are for a fixed period and earn higher interest; premature withdrawal attracts a penalty.

Recurring deposits require a fixed amount to be deposited every month for a fixed period, encouraging regular saving among salaried people and students. Savings and current deposits are demand deposits, while fixed and recurring deposits are time deposits.
section-109: Parties to a cheque are the drawer (account holder who writes it), the drawee (the bank) and the payee (the person to be paid). A cheque must be in writing, unconditional, signed, for a fixed sum and payable on demand.

Types: bearer cheque (payable to whoever presents it), order cheque (payable to a named person or their order), crossed cheque (with two parallel lines, payable only through a bank account) and account payee cheque. A cheque is valid for three months from its date. CTS (Cheque Truncation System) enables faster clearing.
section-110: The pass book shows the date, particulars, withdrawals, deposits and balance of a customer's account. It helps the customer check the accuracy of the account and serves as a record of savings.
Today many banks provide e-passbooks and account statements through internet and mobile banking, but printed passbooks are still common in rural areas and for small savings accounts.
section-111: A demand draft is purchased by paying the amount and commission to the bank. It is drawn by one branch on another branch (or bank) and is payable on demand. Since the money is paid in advance, a DD cannot be dishonoured for lack of funds.
DDs are used for paying fees, applications and transfers where the receiver wants guaranteed payment. They are safer than carrying cash, but are being replaced by NEFT, RTGS and UPI transfers.
section-112: Debit cards allow withdrawal of cash at ATMs and payment at shops and online, with the amount immediately deducted from the account. Credit cards allow 'buy now, pay later' within a credit limit; if the bill is paid within the free credit period no interest is charged, otherwise high interest applies.

Both are called plastic money. They reduce the need to carry cash and support digital transactions. RuPay is India's domestic card network. Risks include fraud, overspending and debt in the case of credit cards.
section-113: Internet banking allows customers to check balances, transfer funds through NEFT, RTGS and IMPS, pay bills, open fixed deposits and request cheque books through the bank's website. Mobile banking provides similar services through apps and SMS.

The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched by NPCI in 2016, has made mobile payments very popular in India. Advantages include 24x7 availability, speed and low cost. Users must protect their passwords, PINs and OTPs to prevent cyber fraud.
section-114: Digital currency may be private (such as cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, which are not legal tender in India) or issued by a central bank. A Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) is legal tender in digital form; the RBI launched pilots of the digital rupee (e-rupee) in 2022 for wholesale and retail use.
Benefits include lower costs of printing and handling cash, faster settlement and financial inclusion. Concerns include privacy, cyber security and the effect on bank deposits.
section-115: Co-operative banks are registered under co-operative societies acts and regulated by the RBI under the Banking Regulation Act. Rural co-operative credit has a short-term structure (State Co-operative Bank, District Central Co-operative Bank and Primary Agricultural Credit Society) and a long-term structure (State and Primary Co-operative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks). Urban co-operative banks serve towns.

They provide cheap credit to farmers, artisans and small businesses. Weaknesses include dual control, political interference, poor recovery and weak governance. In Mizoram, the Mizoram Co-operative Apex Bank serves this role.
section-116: Development banks are also called development financial institutions (DFIs). Besides lending, they provide underwriting, technical advice, project appraisal and promotion of entrepreneurs.
Indian examples include IFCI (1948), ICICI (1955, now a commercial bank), IDBI (1964), NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank and NHB. A new DFI, NaBFID, was created in 2021 for infrastructure financing.
section-117: The Small Industries Development Bank of India was established in 1990 under an Act of Parliament as a subsidiary of IDBI and later became independent. Its head office is in Lucknow.

It refinances banks for MSME loans, gives direct assistance, supports micro-finance institutions, runs the MUDRA refinance window and credit guarantee schemes (CGTMSE), and promotes entrepreneurship development. It helps small firms which find it difficult to get credit.
section-118: The Industrial Development Bank of India was set up in 1964 as a subsidiary of the RBI and became the apex institution for industrial finance in 1976. It provided project finance, refinance and coordination among financial institutions.
In 2004 it was converted into a commercial bank, IDBI Bank Ltd. In 2019 LIC acquired a majority stake, and the government has moved toward its strategic disinvestment.
section-119: The Export-Import Bank of India was established in 1982 and started operations in 1982 under the EXIM Bank Act 1981. Its head office is in Mumbai.

It provides export credit, finance for overseas investment, lines of credit to foreign governments, guarantees, and advisory services. It helps Indian exporters compete in international markets and promotes India's trade relations.
section-120: The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development was set up on 12 July 1982 on the recommendation of the CRAFICARD (Shivaraman) Committee. Its head office is in Mumbai.

Functions: refinance to co-operative banks, RRBs and commercial banks for rural lending; investment credit for rural infrastructure through the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF); supervision of RRBs and co-operative banks; promotion of SHG-bank linkage; and research and planning for rural credit.
section-121: NHB was established in 1988 under the National Housing Bank Act 1987 as a wholly owned subsidiary of the RBI; it is now wholly owned by the Government of India. Its headquarters is in New Delhi.

It refinances housing finance companies and banks, promotes affordable and rural housing, publishes the RESIDEX housing price index and earlier regulated housing finance companies (regulation was transferred to the RBI in 2019).
section-122: A financial market brings together lenders (savers) and borrowers (investors). Its functions include mobilising savings, price discovery, providing liquidity, reducing transaction costs and allocating capital efficiently.

It can be classified into the money market (short-term) and capital market (long-term), organised and unorganised markets, and the foreign exchange market. In India the RBI regulates the money market and SEBI regulates the capital market.
section-123: The money market deals in instruments with maturity up to one year. Participants include the RBI, commercial banks, financial institutions, mutual funds and corporations.

It provides liquidity to banks and businesses, helps the government meet short-term needs and helps the RBI implement monetary policy. The Indian money market has an organised sector (RBI, banks) and an unorganised sector (moneylenders, indigenous bankers).
section-124: The capital market mobilises long-term savings for industry and government. Its main parts are the primary market (new issues), the secondary market (stock exchanges) and the government securities market. Participants include companies, investors, banks, mutual funds, insurance companies and foreign investors.
It promotes capital formation and economic growth. In India it is regulated by SEBI. Major stock exchanges are the Bombay Stock Exchange (1875) and the National Stock Exchange (1992).
section-125: In the primary market, companies raise capital directly from investors through IPOs (initial public offers), follow-on public offers, rights issues and private placements. Funds go to the issuing company.

In the secondary market, investors trade existing shares through stock exchanges; the company receives no new money. The secondary market provides liquidity and price information, which encourages people to invest in the primary market.
section-126: Call money is overnight borrowing and lending between banks; notice money is for 2 to 14 days. Treasury Bills are short-term government securities of 91, 182 and 364 days, issued at a discount. Commercial paper is an unsecured promissory note issued by companies with good credit ratings.

Commercial bills are bills of exchange drawn by sellers on buyers for goods sold on credit and can be discounted with banks. Trade bills arise from trade transactions. Certificates of deposit, issued by banks, are another money-market instrument.
section-127: Equity shares give ownership rights, voting rights and dividends that depend on profits. Preference shares receive a fixed dividend before equity shareholders. Debentures are loans to a company carrying fixed interest; holders are creditors, not owners.

Bonds are long-term debt instruments issued by governments or companies. Other instruments include mutual fund units and derivatives. Each instrument offers a different combination of risk, return and liquidity.
section-128: A stock exchange is an organised market where shares, debentures and bonds are bought and sold under regulations. Trading now takes place electronically with shares held in demat form in depositories such as NSDL and CDSL.

Important indices are the Sensex (BSE, 30 companies) and the Nifty 50 (NSE). Functions include providing liquidity, valuing securities, mobilising savings, ensuring safety of transactions and serving as a barometer of the economy.
section-129: SEBI was set up in 1988 and given statutory powers in 1992 under the SEBI Act. Its headquarters is in Mumbai.

Functions: protective (preventing insider trading and fraud, educating investors), regulatory (registering brokers, mutual funds and merchant bankers, regulating takeovers) and developmental (promoting fair and efficient markets, introducing new products). Its aim is investor protection and healthy development of the securities market.
section-130: The market began in the 1950s, mainly in London, when dollar deposits were held in European banks. The term now covers dollar deposits anywhere outside the USA; similar markets exist for other currencies (Eurocurrency market).

It provides international liquidity, finances trade and investment and allows banks to borrow and lend across borders with fewer regulations. However, it may also contribute to speculative capital flows and global financial instability.
section-132: Evolution: Indian banking grew from indigenous bankers to the Presidency Banks, the Imperial Bank (1921) and the SBI (1955). The RBI was established in 1935. Bank nationalisation (1969 and 1980) spread branches to villages and promoted priority-sector lending. The reforms after 1991 introduced private banks, capital adequacy norms and competition; recent years have seen bank mergers, payments banks, small finance banks and digital banking.

Functions of the central bank: issue of currency, banker to the government, bankers' bank and lender of last resort, custodian of foreign exchange reserves, clearing house, controller of credit, and developmental functions such as promoting rural credit and financial inclusion.

Credit control: Quantitative methods - bank rate, repo and reverse repo rates, open market operations, CRR and SLR - control the total volume of credit. Qualitative methods - margin requirements, consumer credit regulation, credit rationing, moral suasion and direct action - control its direction.

Monetary policy: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee, created in 2016, sets the repo rate to keep CPI inflation at 4 per cent (within 2 to 6 per cent) while supporting growth. Expansionary policy lowers rates; contractionary policy raises them. Effectiveness is limited by the informal sector, time lags and supply shocks such as food and oil prices.
section-133: Money: Money is anything generally acceptable as a medium of exchange. It removed the difficulties of barter. Its functions are primary (medium of exchange, measure of value), secondary (store of value, standard of deferred payments, transfer of value) and contingent (basis of credit, liquidity). Kinds include commodity, metallic, paper, bank, plastic and digital money.

Commercial banks: Their primary functions are accepting deposits and lending money through loans, cash credit, overdrafts and bill discounting; secondary functions are agency and utility services. Credit creation takes place because banks keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves; the credit multiplier equals 1 divided by the reserve ratio.

Deposits and instruments: Savings, current, fixed and recurring deposits suit different customers. A cheque is an order to a bank to pay; a demand draft is a pre-paid bank instrument; the passbook records transactions.

Modern banking: Debit and credit cards, internet banking, mobile banking, UPI, NEFT, RTGS and IMPS make payments quick and convenient. Digital currency, especially the RBI's e-rupee (CBDC), represents the next stage. These developments support a less-cash economy but require cyber security and financial literacy.
section-134: Co-operative banks: They follow the principle of mutual help and serve farmers, artisans and small traders. The short-term rural structure has three tiers - State Co-operative Banks, District Central Co-operative Banks and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies. They face problems of dual control, poor recovery, political interference and lack of professional management.

Development banks: These specialised institutions provide long-term finance and promotional services. SIDBI (1990) supports MSMEs; IDBI (1964) was the apex body of industrial finance before becoming a commercial bank in 2004; EXIM Bank (1982) finances foreign trade; NABARD (1982) is the apex body for agriculture and rural development; NHB (1988) promotes housing finance.

Role: They fill gaps left by commercial banks, finance risky and long-gestation projects, promote entrepreneurship, support balanced regional development and help achieve national priorities. With the liberalisation of the financial sector, some DFIs converted into banks, but new institutions such as NaBFID show their continued importance.
section-135: Meaning and functions: Financial markets bring savers and borrowers together, mobilise savings, discover prices, provide liquidity and reduce transaction costs.

Money market: Deals in short-term funds up to one year. Instruments include call and notice money, Treasury Bills (91, 182, 364 days), commercial paper, certificates of deposit and commercial or trade bills. The RBI regulates it and uses it for monetary policy.

Capital market: Deals in long-term funds. The primary market issues new securities through IPOs and rights issues; the secondary market trades existing securities on exchanges such as BSE and NSE. Instruments include equity and preference shares, debentures and bonds. The Sensex and Nifty indicate market trends.

Regulation and international markets: SEBI (1988, statutory in 1992) protects investors and regulates intermediaries. The Eurodollar market consists of US-dollar deposits outside the USA and provides international liquidity. Well-developed financial markets are essential for capital formation and economic growth.
